facts.claim: Singapore's National Heritage Board inventory says most Chinese wedding practices today begin with a betrothal ceremony called guo da li, held two to four weeks before the wedding on an auspicious day, when the groom, with a female relative, brings gifts to the bride's family.
facts.quote: Most Chinese wedding practices today begin with a betrothal ceremony called guo da li (过大礼). It is held two to four weeks on an auspicious day before the actual wedding day, and involves the groom, accompanied by a female relative, bringing gifts to the bride's family.

facts.claim: The bride's family returns some of the gifts (hui li) to show acceptance of the marriage, presents the groom's family another set of gifts, and the bride receives her trousseau (jia zhuang).
facts.quote: The bride's family then returns some of these gifts, known as hui li (回礼), to symbolise the acceptance of the marriage. They also present the groom's family another set of gifts. This is also when the bride receives her trousseau, known as jia zhuang (嫁妝).

facts.claim: Betrothal gifts are chosen for their symbolism; the source's examples are mandarin oranges for good luck and charcoal for a good life after marriage.
facts.quote: The gifts exchanged are usually elaborate, with items chosen specifically for their symbolism. For example, mandarin oranges are given for good luck, while charcoal signifies a good life after marriage.

facts.claim: The night before the wedding, a hair-combing ritual (shang tou) marks the couple's transition into adulthood; it takes place in both homes, each facing a pair of lighted candles while a woman of good fortune combs the hair four times, repeating an auspicious phrase each time.
facts.quote: The night before the wedding includes a hair-combing ritual called shang tou (上头) to symbolise the couple's transition into adulthood. The ritual takes place in the respective homes of the groom and the bride. Each of them faces a pair of lighted candles while a woman considered to have good fortune (someone whose husband, children, and grandchildren are alive) combs the hair four times and repeats an auspicious phrase each time.

facts.claim: On the wedding day the groom goes to fetch the bride, but first the bridesmaids set the groom and groomsmen a series of playful tasks ('gatecrashing') before he can see her.
facts.quote: On the wedding day, the groom goes to the bride's home to bring her back to his home. But first, there is a ritual called "gatecrashing", where the bridesmaids make the groom and his groomsmen complete a series of playful tasks before he can see the bride.

facts.claim: A Singapore wedding planner quoted in the inventory says Teochew families believe the bride should leave home before sunrise, so they hold the gatecrash very early in the morning.
facts.quote: The Teochews believe that the bride should leave her home before sunrise, and thus hold the gatecrash ritual very early in the morning.

facts.claim: The first tea ceremony is at the groom's home: where deities and ancestors are worshipped at home, the couple pray at the family altar, then serve tea to the family elders, who give their blessings.
facts.quote: The first part of the tea ceremony then takes place at the groom's home. If deities and ancestors are worshipped at home, the couple will pray at the family altar before serving tea to the elders of the family. The elders will give their blessings to the couple.

facts.claim: The couple then hold a separate tea ceremony for the bride's family at her house, after the bride changes into a kua, a red wedding dress embroidered with auspicious symbols.
facts.quote: The couple then leave for the bride's house to hold a separate tea ceremony for the bride's family, after the bride changes into a kua (褂). The kua is a traditional red Chinese wedding dress embroidered with auspicious symbols.

facts.claim: Each dialect group has its own distinct wedding practices, and many couples have simplified some rituals because of modernisation, busy schedules and budgets.
facts.quote: They also help to reinforce the ethnic identity of the participants, especially that of dialect groups since each group has its distinct wedding practices. ... Over time, modernisation, busy schedules and budget constraints have led some to the simplification of certain rituals.

facts.claim: The matrimonial bed is prepared (an chuang) three days to one week before the wedding with new red-tray items for prosperity; on the day a young boy is asked to jump and roll on the bed to bless the couple with children.
facts.quote: The next step is preparing the matrimonial bed in a ritual known as an chuang (安床). This takes place three days to one week before the wedding. ... On the wedding day, before the bridal couple arrive, a young boy (ideally one born in the Year of the Dragon) is asked to jump and roll on the matrimonial bed as a way to bless the couple with many children.

facts.claim: Singapore's National Library Board says Chinese wedding customs vary by dialect group and that, despite simplification, a wedding is often not considered complete until the customary rites are performed.
facts.quote: Chinese wedding customs and tradition generally vary according to dialect group. Although modernisation has resulted in the simplification of traditional marriage rituals, a Chinese wedding is often not considered complete until the couple have performed the customary rites.

facts.claim: Matching the couple's horoscopes and using professional matchmakers are rarely practised today, but presenting betrothal gifts (guo da li) is still observed.
facts.quote: The traditional ritual of matching the horoscopes of the couple before a marriage to ensure compatibility, along with the custom of using professional matchmakers to plan the wedding arrangements, is rarely practised today. However, the custom of presenting betrothal gifts to the bride's family as a token of appreciation – in a ceremony known as guo da li – is still being observed by couples.

facts.claim: By custom, betrothal gifts are presented on an auspicious day, usually chosen from the tongshu (Chinese almanac); the groom's family brings food items and gifts symbolising good luck and prosperity.
facts.quote: According to Chinese custom, the presentation of betrothal gifts should be carried out on an auspicious day – usually chosen from the tongshu (Chinese almanac) – one to two weeks prior to the date of the wedding ceremony. During guo da li, the groom's family presents the bride's family with food items and gifts that symbolise good luck and prosperity.

facts.claim: Gifts differ by dialect group: Teochew gifts typically include peanut-sesame candy wrapped in red paper; Cantonese families may send seafood such as sea cucumber, abalone, scallop, dried shrimp, oyster, mushroom and fish maw.
facts.quote: In Teochew weddings, typical gifts include pieces of peanut-sesame candy wrapped in red paper to signify qian zi wan sun ("a thousand children, ten thousand grandchildren") ... For the Cantonese, the bride's family may be given seafood such as sea cucumber, cuttlefish, abalone, scallop, shark's fin, dried shrimp, oyster, mushroom and fish maw.

facts.claim: Common across dialect groups are two pairs of red dragon and phoenix candles; the groom's parents may give the bride dragon and phoenix bangles (Cantonese) or four items of gold jewellery, si dian jin (Teochew).
facts.quote: Items common across the dialect groups include two pairs of red dragon and phoenix candles, with the dragon representing the groom and the phoenix representing the bride. The groom's parents may also give the bride jewellery: a pair of dragon and phoenix bangles for the Cantonese, and four items of gold jewellery (si dian jin) –a pair of earrings, a ring, bangle and necklace – for the Teochews.

facts.claim: The hair-combing ritual is held at an auspicious hour in each home, with blessings spoken at each stroke; traditionally Cantonese, it is also practised by other dialect groups in Singapore, and may be performed by parents or a happily married elder female relative.
facts.quote: Although this has traditionally been a Cantonese custom, other dialect groups in Singapore also practise it. The ceremony may be performed by the parents of the bride and groom, or an elderly or respected female relative, one who is happily married and has many children and grandchildren.

facts.claim: After the hair-combing, the bride and groom eat a bowl of glutinous rice balls.
facts.quote: After the ceremony, the bride and groom eat a bowl of glutinous rice balls, which symbolise togetherness in their relationship.

facts.claim: At the bride's door, her female friends and relatives (jie mei, 'sisters') will not let the groom and his entourage in until he meets their demands, including a red packet and publicly declaring his love in novel ways.
facts.quote: At the door to the bride's home, the groom and his buddies are greeted by a boisterous group of the bride's female relatives and friends called jie mei, or "sisters", who will not let him in unless he accedes to their demands. ... To add to the fun and gaiety of the occasion, the groom is also made to publicly declare his love in novel ways before the "sisters" allow him entry into the house.

facts.claim: At the groom's home the tea ceremony officially recognises the couple as husband and wife after the 'three bows': to heaven and earth, to parents, and to each other.
facts.quote: At the groom's home, the couple performs the "tea ceremony", a ritual that officially recognises the couple as husband and wife after they've performed the "three bows". The first bow is directed to heaven and earth, the second to parents and the third to each other.

facts.claim: The tea is usually brewed with lotus seeds, two red dates and two longans.
facts.quote: The tea served is usually brewed with lotus seeds, two red dates and two longans to symbolise a sweet and fertile marriage.

facts.claim: Order of serving: tea is offered first to the gods, then the groom's ancestors, then the groom's parents, then senior family members and other relatives; those served sit while the couple kneel (or bow) and offer the cup with both hands, and each person served gives a red packet or jewellery.
facts.quote: Tea is first offered to the gods and then to the groom's ancestors to obtain blessings. Next, tea is served to the groom's parents followed by senior members of the family and other relatives. Those who are served tea are usually seated, while the couple kneels and offers the tea cup using both hands. Some couples, however, choose to bow instead of kneeling when serving the tea. ... Everyone who is served gives the couple a hongbao or jewellery item.

facts.claim: In the old days the return visit to the bride's family was made after three days; today the bride returns home on the wedding day itself and the tea ceremony is performed for her parents and relatives.
facts.quote: After the tea ceremony at the groom's house, the couple returns to the bride's house. In the old days, the return visit is made after three days ... Today, the bride returns home on the wedding day itself, and the tea ceremony is then performed on her parents and relatives.

facts.claim: Historically the groom presented a whole roast pig to his in-laws on the return visit; the meat was shared among the bride's relatives and the head and tail returned to the groom for 'a good beginning and end'.
facts.quote: In the old days, the return visit is made after three days, by which time the marriage would have been consummated and the groom presents a whole roast pig to his in-laws ... The pig is cut up and the meat distributed to the bride's relatives, and the head and tail are then returned to the groom to signify "a good beginning and end" to the marriage.

facts.claim: Hotel function rooms tend to be fully booked on dates seen as auspicious (the source cites 8 August 2008, 9 September 2009 and 10 October 2010).
facts.quote: As many couples prefer to hold the banquet in a hotel function room, these venues tend to be fully booked on auspicious dates such as 8 August 2008, 9 September 2009 and 10 October 2010 despite the fact that receptions cost more on these dates.

facts.claim: The bride's father traditionally places the bridal veil on his daughter's head to mark her coming of age, before the groom collects her.
facts.quote: It is a tradition that the father places the bridal veil on his daughter's head to mark her coming of age.

facts.claim: The National Museum of Singapore describes san zhao hui men as a traditional element of a Chinese wedding in which the bride returns to her home with the groom on the third day after the wedding; its example garment dates from 1952.
facts.quote: This piece was worn by Lucy Chan on the third day after her wedding to Chan Ah Kow for san zhao hui men (三朝回门) - a traditional element of a Chinese wedding in which the bride returns to her home with the groom

facts.region: China (general; source says customs varied region to region)
facts.claim: A community heritage summary says the Book of Rites, the Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial and the Baihu Tong outline the 'Three Covenants and the Six Rites', and that even in the Warring States period the full ritual was simplified; it does not list the six rites by name.
facts.quote: Three venerable texts, The Book of Rites, The Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial, and the Baihu Tong outline the Three Covenants and the Six Rites, that were considered necessary elements of a marriage. However, the full ritual was so complicated that even within the span of the Warring States period, the etiquette underwent changes and simplification.
facts.conflicts: Chinese Historical and Cultural Project (US non-profit) states its own page 'is by no means a scholarly work'; cite as a community heritage summary, not as authority; its bibliography includes a Hong Kong Museum of History publication.

facts.claim: The same summary says customs varied across China from region to region and even village to village.
facts.quote: Moreover, there were variations across China's vast expanse – from region to region and even village to village.
facts.conflicts: Chinese Historical and Cultural Project (US non-profit) states its own page 'is by no means a scholarly work'; cite as a community heritage summary, not as authority; its bibliography includes a Hong Kong Museum of History publication.

facts.claim: Historically, betrothal gifts included tea, dragon and phoenix bridal cakes, paired poultry, sweetmeats and wine; in some areas the gifts were collectively called cha-li ('tea presents'), and the bride's family reciprocated with food and clothing.
facts.quote: The boy's family presented betrothal gifts of money and significant items such as tea, "Dragon (male) and Phoenix (female)" bridal cakes, pairs of male and female poultry, sweetmeats and sugar, wine and tobacco ... Tea was such a primary part of these gifts in some areas that they were known collectively as cha-li, that is, "tea presents." The girl's family reciprocated with gifts of food and clothing.
facts.conflicts: Chinese Historical and Cultural Project (US non-profit) states its own page 'is by no means a scholarly work'; cite as a community heritage summary, not as authority; its bibliography includes a Hong Kong Museum of History publication.

facts.claim: The bride's family traditionally shared the bridal cakes with friends and relatives as an announcement of and invitation to the wedding feast.
facts.quote: It was customary for the girl's family to distribute the bridal cakes they received from the boy's family to friends and relatives as a form of announcement and invitation to the wedding feast.
facts.conflicts: Chinese Historical and Cultural Project (US non-profit) states its own page 'is by no means a scholarly work'; cite as a community heritage summary, not as authority; its bibliography includes a Hong Kong Museum of History publication.

facts.claim: Auspicious wedding days are interpreted by fortune tellers from the couple's birth date and hour after consulting the Chinese almanac, and self-analysis from the almanac is considered bad form.
facts.quote: Auspicious days are subject to interpretation by fortune tellers that perform the analysis based on one's birth date (day and hour) after consultation with the Chinese almanac. ... In the Chinese community it is considered bad form if an individual consults the almanac and performs a self analysis.
facts.conflicts: Chinese Historical and Cultural Project (US non-profit) states its own page 'is by no means a scholarly work'; cite as a community heritage summary, not as authority; its bibliography includes a Hong Kong Museum of History publication.

facts.claim: Historically, about three days after the wedding the couple visited the bride's family home, where she was received as a guest.
facts.quote: In general, three days after the wedding, the couple paid a visit to the bride's family home, where the bride is now received as a guest.
facts.conflicts: Chinese Historical and Cultural Project (US non-profit) states its own page 'is by no means a scholarly work'; cite as a community heritage summary, not as authority; its bibliography includes a Hong Kong Museum of History publication.

facts.claim: Historically, the bride's friends would not 'surrender' the bride until satisfied with red packets (ang pau) from the groom's representative, with good-natured haggling.
facts.quote: On arriving at the bride's house, the groom's party was met by the bride's friends, who would not 'surrender ' the bride until they were satisfied by red packets of money, ang pau from the groom's representative. This was the occasion of much good-natured haggling before the two parties could reach an agreement.
facts.conflicts: Chinese Historical and Cultural Project (US non-profit) states its own page 'is by no means a scholarly work'; cite as a community heritage summary, not as authority; its bibliography includes a Hong Kong Museum of History publication.

often_told: Names and order of the six rites (proposal, birth-date exchange, betrothal gifts, wedding gifts, date setting, fetching the bride) and the three letters (betrothal, gift, wedding letters): often told; no source read today lists them, so name the classical sequence only as 'often told' and cite fact_27 for the Book of Rites framing.
Wording of the four hair-combing blessings: often told; sources confirm four strokes with an auspicious phrase each time (fact_04) but not the words.
Months or dates to avoid (for example the seventh lunar month, Hungry Ghost period, mentioned in the CHCP summary): often told, describe lightly.
Pairs of items, lucky numbers in gift counts and red-packet sums: often told; do not state (amounts banned).
The term pin li and its meaning: often told; sources read use guo da li (Singapore) and cha-li (historical, some areas).
Groom's family offering tea to the bride's parents first, or Hokkien-specific tea order: often told.

insider_details.detail: Plan the tea ceremony as two sittings, one at each family home, since sources describe a ceremony at the groom's home and a separate one for the bride's family on the same day; build travel time between homes into the run sheet.

If either family is Teochew, ask early whether they want the bride to leave home before sunrise, because that puts the door games very early in the morning and pushes hair and make-up into the small hours.

Auspicious dates draw demand: Singapore's National Library notes hotel function rooms book out on dates seen as lucky, so families choosing a date by almanac or fortune teller should lock venues as soon as the date is set.

Brief the photographer and the elder seated for tea: the couple usually kneel (some bow) and offer the cup with both hands, and a helper refills cups on a red tray, so allow floor space and a cushion.
Ask both families which rites they want rather than assuming a set list, since customs differ by dialect group and many couples simplify them.
